newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Big hurdles face Yeltsin in "Buy Russian" campaign.
newsitem.headline: Big hurdles face Yeltsin in "Buy Russian" campaign.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin reaped some immediate political capital on Tuesday from a new "Buy Russian" campaign but politicians and analysts played down the chances of any rapid economic gains.

Yeltsin's appeal for Russians to buy domestic goods instead of imports was the latest effort by the Kremlin leader to regain his place as paramount leader, partly by tackling economic problems, after months off the scene with ill health.

The call crossed political barriers, just as a new crusade against corruption has a broad appeal, and appealed at least as much to nationalists and communists as his more traditional liberal supporters.

"Yeltsin is showing himself searching for a way out of the economic crisis and making up for his long absence," said Irina Kobrinskaya, a political analyst at the Moscow office of the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace.

Admiring Yeltsin's delivery of the radio address, in which he recalled his pride in giving his wife Russian-made white gym shoes many years ago, she said: "Neither the left, the right, the communists or anyone can be against this."

Since he returned to the Kremlin less than two months ago after heart problems followed by pneumonia, Yeltsin has been trying to reassert his grip on power and show a firm hand. He has criticised those around him and reshuffled the government.

In his sixth year in office, and almost a year into his second and final presidential term, the 66-year-old Kremlin leader is trying to shake off the image as a destroyer which he gained by helping end communist rule and bury the Soviet Union.
Many political commentators say he now wants to show he is a creator, or builder, by putting economic reforms on track and uniting Russians of all political colours behind his efforts.
Opposition politicians reacted positively to the idea behind his campaign, just as they welcomed his declaration of war on corruption through gritted teeth earlier this month.
"I have to admit that this time the president is playing on the people's side and doing the right thing," Valentin Varennikov, a communist member of parliament, said.
"It is a step in the right direction. He has started thinking positively," conservative Agrarian leader Nikolai Kharitonov said begrudgingly.
But even some of the politicians who welcomed the campaign gave it little chance of a quick success in economic terms.
A glance at any of the thousands of street kiosks in Moscow provides a clue to the size of the task Yeltsin faces.

The kiosks are monuments to the growth of private enterprise and the economic changes since the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991, but Russians goods are often hard to find alongside the brightly-coloured imported products.
"The campaign is a good thing but it is unclear how effective it will be," said liberal parliamentarian Vladimir Lukin.

"I'll buy domestic goods when they are better and cheaper than foreign ones. You know what choice any normal person will make if he has to choose between domestic goods which are expensive and of poor quality, and good and cheap foreign products."
Critics said Yeltsin must take separate measures to give Russians a reason to buy national products.
They said some foreign companies produce their goods in Russia and provide a source of employment for Russians.
Liberal parliamentarian Sergei Ivanenko called for tax relief to help domestic producers. Centrist deputy Pavel Bunich proposed high customs duties.
But Yeltsin has ruled out protectionist moves, which would risk a row with Western countries that could dent Russia's hopes of joining international trade and economic groups.

Andrei Kortunov, a political analyst who heads the independent Russian Science Foundation, said Yeltsin still had a long way to go to turn his words into deeds and overcome Russians' traditional lack of faith in their leaders.
"These are very fine words but this is very difficult to implement," he said. "I don't think the people are impressed."
